## 1. Introduction

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the consequence of environmental exposures (cigarette smoking and air pollution) and genetic susceptibility. It is potentially both progressive and debilitating but is also preventable by controlling environmental exposures [[Citation 1](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. COPD results in exhaled airflow limitation or air trapping that is not fully reversible. As a clinical syndrome, COPD has variable elements of reversible airway disease, emphysema, and bronchitis with infections and/or excessive sputum production [[Citation 2](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. COPD continues to increase its ranking as a cause of death globally, most recently reaching the third leading cause of death with 3.23 million deaths attributed to it in 2019 [[Citation 1](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 1.1. Prevalence

A systematic review and meta-analysis using 60 papers and 127,598 subjects found that the prevalence of post-bronchodilator airway obstruction was 12.6% (10.91–13.40%) [[Citation 3](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Pooled prevalence of COPD in this 2019 study was 15.7% (13.80–18.59%) in men and 9.93% (8.73–11.13%) in women. Some countries like the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia have seen a 49% increase in the prevalence of COPD in the population between 1990 and 2019 [[Citation 4](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis used 42 studies and found the overall prevalence of COPD in people aged 40 years and older to be 12.64% (95% confidence interval (CI) 10.75–14.65%) to 7.38% (95% CI 5.47–9.55%) depending on the diagnostic criteria used [[Citation 5](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In this study, men also had a higher prevalence of 15.47% (95% CI 12.22–19.02%) versus 8.79% (95% CI 6.94–10.82%) for women. Increased tobacco smoking in women from developed countries and the disproportionate exposure to indoor pollutants such as biomass burning in women from less developed countries have increased the prevalence of COPD in women in the 21 st century, but some evidence suggests women may in fact be more susceptible to tobacco smoke than men [[Citation 6](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 1.2. The burden of COPD

A recent evaluation of the burden of COPD in the United States (US) included 4,135 COPD patients and 86,021 people without COPD [[Citation 7](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Using 2019 US dollars, the COPD-attributed medical cost after adjustments was estimated to be $31.3 billion. They further estimated that by 2029, the costs would essentially double to $60.5 billion [[Citation 7](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

COPD often goes undiagnosed until it is advanced resulting in underestimating its true clinical and societal burden [[Citation 8](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. COPD exacerbations result in increased healthcare use, work absenteeism, and reduced productivity. Studies on mortality have ranged from hazard ratios (HR) of 4.3 (95% CI, 2.8–6.7) for death from respiratory causes to a HR of 2.0 (95% CI, 1.8–2.3) for death of any cause in Denmark [[Citation 9](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. An analysis of US data found that even in patients with undiagnosed COPD, an increased HR for death over 20 years was 1.23 (95% CI, 1.08–1.40) compared to those without COPD [[Citation 10](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In 2023, recently released data suggests that death rates from lower respiratory disease decreased by 12.5% but still remained the fourth leading cause of death in the United States [[Citation 11](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 12](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Exacerbations of COPD predict higher mortality risk [[Citation 13](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. This has resulted in a call for COPD management to be centered around reducing mortality and COPD exacerbations [[Citation 13](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Using the Swedish national register (1997–2018) of all residents between 50 and 90 years-old, patients with a diagnosis of COPD were evaluated [[Citation 14](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Of the 2,706,814 persons in the register, 8.3% had COPD. The investigations used a nested case-control with 223,945 COPD cases and 1,062,731 controls. COPD patients had increased risks for chronic heart failure (odds ratio (OR) = 3.25, 95% CI 3.20–3.30), peripheral arterial disease (OR = 3.12, 95% CI 3.06–3.18), and lung cancer (OR = 12.73, 95% CI 12.12–13.37). After the diagnosis had formally been made, an increased risk of depression was also found (HR = 2.58, 95% CI 2.53–2.64). Interstitial lung disease, emphysema, bronchiectasis, osteoporosis, and cardiovascular events have also been associated with COPD [[Citation 15–17](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 1.3. Therapy for COPD

This paper will focus on the pharmacotherapy used in treating COPD patients with an emphasis on newer agents. The frequently updated Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) is a strategy document for the diagnosis, treatment and management of COPD patients and offers a comprehensive review of available treatments of COPD [[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. This review is limited to pharmacotherapy but this in no way downplays the importance of non-lung pharmacological directed approaches such as smoking cessation, airway valves, pulmonary rehabilitation, nutrition, oxygen therapy, and general lifestyle interventions in the comprehensive treatment of COPD [[Citation 19–22](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

## 2. Bronchodilators

Inhaled bronchodilators such as beta2-agonists and anti-muscarinics are a cornerstone of treatment for airway diseases, including COPD. Despite multiple new therapies, inhaled bronchodilators remain integral in the management of COPD in alleviating symptoms, improving lung function, and decreasing the rate of exacerbations. Inhaled beta2-agonists have been shown to improve forced expiatory volume in 1 second (FEV1), reduce dynamic hyperinflation, improve specific total airway resistance, improve exercise tolerance, and improve dyspnea and health-related quality of life scores. [[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 23](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 24](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In this review, recent advancements and data on bronchodilators are presented. Table 1 provides a comprehensive summary of inhaled bronchodilators.

### Table 1.  FDA-approved long-acting beta2-agonist and anti-muscarinic inhaled medications, including common brand names and combination inhalers.

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0001&doi=10.1080%2F14656566.2024.2409322&downloadType=CSV)[Display Table](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)

The relationship of frequency of dosing to adherence has clearly been shown to be an inverse relationship with increasing frequency for oral agents [[Citation 25](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The relationship of frequency of required inhaler dosing and adherence is less clear in COPD patients [[Citation 25](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Once-a-day ICS/LABA/LAMA inhaler in COPD patients was shown to be non-inferior to twice-a-day ICS/LABA plus once-a-day LAMA [[Citation 26](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Once-a-day ICS/LAMA/LABA inhaler use in COPD has been shown to have significantly improved adherence compared to multiple-inhaler triple therapy [[Citation 27](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A large study that included both asthma and COPD patients demonstrated that 80% or greater adherence was seen in the 1,791 COPD patients given once-a-day medication compared to twice-a-day inhalers (54.8% vs 38.6%, _p_< 0.001) [[Citation 28](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Inhaler adherence even with the use of once-a-day inhalers remains a problem.

### 2.1. Beta2-agonists

Long-acting beta2-agonists (LABAs), such as formoterol and salmeterol, provide sustained bronchodilation by stimulating beta2-adrenergic receptors on airway smooth muscle cells, leading to the activation of adenylate cyclase and subsequent increase in cyclic AMP levels, which relaxes bronchial smooth muscle [[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. This relaxation causes the airway passages to widen, reducing airway resistance and facilitating easier ventilation [[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Inhaled LABAs have also been shown to simulate airway cilia improving ciliary movement [[Citation 29](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Beta2-agonists are categorized by the length of their clinical effect; inhaled short-acting beta2-agonists (SABA) and long-acting beta2-agonists (LABA) are major classifications.

While inhaled and targeted to the lung, beta2-agonists can lead to off-target effects, including tremors, hypokalemia, and cardiac arrhythmia [[Citation 30](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Identifying the causality of arrhythmias is challenging, as cardiovascular disease is more commonly observed in patients with COPD independent of beta2-agonist medications [[Citation 31](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Patients diagnosed with COPD are significantly more likely to have atrial fibrillation/flutter and ventricular tachycardia than those without COPD [[Citation 32](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A 2015 meta-analysis demonstrated patients with COPD were over twice as likely (odds ratio (OR) 2.46; 95% CI 2.02–3.00) to develop cardiovascular disease when compared to matched cohorts, highlighting the need for careful attention to cardiac disease and risk in patients with COPD [[Citation 33](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Despite these data and up to a third of patients with COPD dying of cardiac disease, a 2022 Canadian cohort demonstrated the exact opposite. Compared to a matched non-COPD cohort, patients with COPD achieved guideline-directed cardiac risk factor monitoring and management [[Citation 34](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. While some trials suggest an association between the use of LABAs and cardiovascular disease, the long-term experience with these medications is reassuring [[Citation 35](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Inhaled SABA use can exert minor effects on β1 receptors in the heart, leading to tachycardia and arrhythmias. Levalbuterol, an (R)-enantiomer of albuterol, may reduce the more cardio-specific effects from the (S)-enantiomer, with the former predominantly responsible for the bronchodilator effects. In comparison, albuterol is a racemic mixture of the (R) and (S) isomers. While levalbuterol appears to be ideal, cost and the lack of demonstrable clinical benefit have limited supplanting albuterol as the first-line SABA [[Citation 36](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 2.2. Anti-muscarinics

Inhaled anti-muscarinic medications such as the quaternary amines tiotropium and ipratropium achieve bronchodilation by antagonizing muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, thereby blocking the action of acetylcholine and preventing smooth muscle contraction [[Citation 23](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The cholinergic system in the lung affects smooth muscle contraction, but also inflammation in the airway epithelium and mucous secretion from goblet cells and submucosal glands [[Citation 37](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Inhaled anti-muscarinics are antagonists of the muscarinic type 1 receptor (M1) and muscarinic type 3 receptor (M3), block mucous production of mucus, and result in relaxation of bronchial smooth muscles in the airway thus reversing acetylcholine-mediated bronchospasms [[Citation 38](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Selectivity of blocking M3 and M1 over M2 receptors is key with M2 receptor stimulation resulting in presynaptic M2 auto-receptors that inhibit excessive acetylcholine release and increase acetylcholine mediated airway contractions. Long-acting anti-muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) are often first-line therapy in patients with COPD. For patients with low symptom burden (GOLD group A), LAMA use may be superior to LABA therapy [[Citation 39](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Data (and experience) show that the addition of short-acting anti-muscarinic (SAMA) to long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) can increase exercise capacity and improve lung function and symptoms [[Citation 40](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The use of SAMA is more debatable in the context of regular LAMA use. Adding a SAMA does show benefits in lung function in this context but is generally avoided due to higher rates of anti-muscarinic side effects, especially urinary retention in men with known prostatic hypertrophy, and theoretical concern for competitive binding with the LAMA [[Citation 41](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 42](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Like beta2-agonists, it is not clear if LAMA use is associated with increased cardiac disease, as stimulation of the M 2 receptor is associated with tachycardia [[Citation 43](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Post-hoc analysis of the ASCENT-COPD trial showed no increased cardiac events in patients with known cardiac disease given LAMA and LABA [[Citation 43](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

In a large comparative effectiveness study, multiple combined inhalers with combinations of various LAMA and LABA agents demonstrated a reduction in exacerbation rate and pneumonia compared to salmeterol/fluticasone propionate (HR .73, 95% CI, 0.59–0.90), although there was a significant variance between other LABA/inhaled corticosteroid combinations and inhaled LAMA/LABA agents [[Citation 44](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 2.3. Inhaled corticosteroids

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), such as fluticasone and budesonide, penetrate airway epithelial cells upon inhalation and bind to intracellular glucocorticoid receptors, forming a complex that then translocates into the nucleus, leading to the transcription of myriad anti-inflammatory pathways such as interleukin-6, mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphatase-1 (MKP-1), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. [[Citation 45](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 46](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In COPD, ICS administered in combination with bronchodilators can up-regulate beta2 receptors, increasing the effect and preventing tachyphylaxis [[Citation 47](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Complementary, the administration of beta2-agonists can increase the translocation of glucocorticosteroids into the nucleus [[Citation 47](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Clinically available ICS (and all corticosteroids (CS) in fact) can vary in potency, duration of action, and systemic bioavailability. These differences can significantly impact their clinical effectiveness and safety profiles. For instance, medications such as fluticasone propionate and budesonide are considered high-potency corticosteroids, requiring lower doses to achieve therapeutic effects due to their strong affinity for glucocorticoid receptors and potent anti-inflammatory actions within the lungs [[Citation 45](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Conversely, low-to-medium-potency corticosteroids like beclomethasone dipropionate and ciclesonide offer effective anti-inflammatory control but with a reduced risk of systemic side effects due to lower bioavailability and faster clearance from the body [[Citation 48](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A study evaluating the differences in efficacy and safety among ICS/LABA combination found that those containing fluticasone had an odds ratio for severe pneumonia of 2.1 while those combination inhalers with budesomide were 1.17 and other ICSs in COPD were 1.41 [[Citation 49](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. These medications may be suitable for patients requiring maintenance therapy with a focus on minimizing systemic corticosteroid exposure, especially in individuals prone to corticosteroid-related adverse effects such as osteoporosis or adrenal suppression.

Low doses of corticosteroids are highly effective at reducing eosinophilic/type 2 inflammation. While this is traditionally associated with asthma, there is considerable concurrence of asthma in COPD and acknowledgment of type 2 inflammation in COPD [[Citation 50](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. COPD has historically been viewed as a predominantly neutrophilic disorder, which requires much higher doses of corticosteroids to modulate [[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

CS have long been an integral part of the management of COPD, due to their potent anti-inflammatory properties, but recent evidence suggests only certain groups of patients may benefit from scheduled ICS. Patients with frequent and/or severe exacerbations appear to benefit most [[Citation 52](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The IMPACT trial demonstrated an approximately 25% reduction in moderate and severe exacerbations with the addition of ICS (the low-to-moderate dose of 100-µg fluticasone furoate) to LAMA/LABA therapy but with an increased HR of 1.53 for pneumonia with the inclusion of ICS [[Citation 53](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In the ETHOS trial, patients received ICS at either 320 μg or 160 μg of budesonide twice per day were compared to ICS/LABA and LAMA/LABA [[Citation 52](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. As in IMPACT, moderate and severe exacerbations were reduced by about 25%, but with no increased risk of pneumonia in this cohort. Notably, ETHOS nor IMPACT demonstrated decreased mortality, but ETHOS has been found to have a high number of patients previously diagnosed with asthma and both suffered from the risk of ICS withdrawal [[Citation 54](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Recent studies have highlighted the role of blood eosinophils as a biomarker for predicting the efficacy of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Elevated blood eosinophil levels have been associated with a better response to ICS therapy. The FLAME study showed that patients with higher eosinophil counts (≥2% or ≥300 cells/µL) experienced a greater reduction in exacerbation rates when treated with ICS in combination with long-acting bronchodilators compared to those with lower eosinophil counts [[Citation 55](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Numerous subsequent post-hoc and pooled analyses have demonstrated both an association with exacerbations and higher peripheral eosinophil levels, in addition to no efficacy of ICS in patients with eosinophils <100 cells/μL [[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. ETHOS showed no benefit of ICS with eosinophils <150 cells/μL. Post-hoc analysis of IMPACT showed benefits for those with prior moderate and severe exacerbations with eosinophils over 100 cells/μL [[Citation 56](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Furthermore, a meta-analysis by Bafadhel et al [[Citation 57](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. confirmed that blood eosinophil levels could predict the likelihood of benefiting from ICS therapy. The 2024 GOLD guidelines recommend ICS in patients with eosinophils over 300 cells/μL and COPD without concurrent asthma or multiple prior cases of pneumonia [[Citation 23](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

In stable COPD, ICS are not shown to improve lung function or mortality [[Citation 58](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Despite GOLD guidelines recommending against the use of ICS in this population, as many as ~40% of group B patients are receiving ICS in practice [[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. There is concern that rapid withdrawal of ICS can induce exacerbation. In a cohort of patients without frequent exacerbation, Patel et al. found no increase in exacerbation after appropriately discontinuing ICS [[Citation 59](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Numerous other clinical trials found an increase in exacerbations after abrupt withdrawal of ICS in patients with prior exacerbations. The available evidence suggests patients can be taken off of ICS without weaning regardless of the severity of lung disease, but not in those patients with a history of exacerbations [[Citation 60](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. While weaning protocols exist, they are uncommonly used in clinical practice [[Citation 60](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

However, the use of ICS in COPD is not without risk. The use of ICS, especially at higher doses, is associated with higher rates of corticosteroid local (candidiasis, dysphonia) and systemic (pneumonia, osteoporosis, glaucoma) adverse effects [[Citation 61](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 62](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Systemic exposure of ICS is primarily determined by drug clearance and bioavailability. All of the clinically available ICS are metabolized in the liver via the CYP enzyme, therefore those with impaired liver function or other CYP modulators should be considered if high dose required. Systemic effects of ICS, though less frequent than with oral corticosteroids, can occur particularly with higher doses, prolonged use, and poor inhaler technique [[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Even adrenal suppression can occur when ICS are used at high doses over extended periods [[Citation 45](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Long-term use of ICS has also been associated with an increased risk of osteoporosis and bone fractures, particularly in elderly patients or those with other risk factors for osteoporosis [[Citation 48](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Diabetes and bone fracture have been associated with high-dose ICS, but the correlation is less clear [[Citation 63](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Multiple studies have shown that ICS use in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is associated with an increased risk of pneumonia. The risk appears to be dose-dependent, with higher doses correlating with greater risk. GOLD and the Canadian Society Recommendations reference this increased risk [[Citation 23](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 64](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A systematic review by Miravitlles et al. also found no increased risk with shorter half-life ICS such as budesonide [[Citation 63](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Careful patient phenotyping selection with monitoring are essential to balance the benefits of inflammation control against the risks of adverse effects. In patients without concurrent asthma, the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease [[Citation 23](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. guidelines recommend using blood eosinophil counts to predict exacerbation risk and tailor ICS treatment [[Citation 23](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Patients experiencing 2 or more moderate or 1 or more severe exacerbations per year with higher eosinophil counts (≥300 cells/µL) are recommended to use ICS therapy and should be considered for triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS). Those without frequent exacerbations and with lower eosinophil counts (≤100 cells/µL) may not benefit as much and face an increased risk of pneumonia from ICS use, therefore ICS should be avoided.

### 2.4. Inhaled drug delivery

In inhaled drugs, medications are paired with a myriad of devices and approaches (Table 3). Therefore, drug delivery to the lungs is of equal importance as the choice of medications. Several key factors, including patient technique, inspiratory flow, manual dexterity, and cognitive and coordination abilities, influence the effectiveness of drug delivery via inhalers. GOLD guidelines emphasize the importance of inhaler education and reevaluation or technique on follow-up. [[Citation 23](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Peak inspiratory flow (PIF) is a point-of-care measurement with increasing clinical usage measuring the inhalation speed and force needed for adequate drug delivery, especially dry powder inhalers (DPI) which require force to deaggregate and disperse the drug. Nearly 25% of patients with observably normal inhaler technique do not have the adequate PIF for their prescribed inhaler [[Citation 65](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Arthritis and other causes of impaired manual dexterity impede a patient’s ability to properly handle and activate the inhaler, especially devices such as the diskus [[Citation 66](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Cognitive and coordination abilities are also essential as patients must understand and accurately follow the inhalation technique, which involves steps such as shaking the inhaler, positioning it correctly, and timing the inhalation with the release of the medication [[Citation 67](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Factors that affect choice of inhaler in COPD are reviewed in more detail [[Citation 68](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. These factors, if not properly managed, can and do lead to reduced treatment efficacy. Despite guidelines and educational efforts focusing on this issue, rates of improper use and inadequate delivery remain high, with as few as 30% of patients with adequate drug delivery [[Citation 69](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Nebulization is an alternative approach to inhalers for respiratory drug delivery. No coordination is required; just simple tidal breathing water-based nebulization results in drugs precipitating out in large airways. While time and effort (cleaning, storage, etc.) are considerably longer with nebulization, patients with barriers to delivery with inhalers, including manual dexterity, cognition, and inspiratory force, can obtain better delivery [[Citation 70](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 2.5. Environmental impact

The environmental impact of inhalers, particularly metered-dose inhalers (MDIs), is significant due to their reliance on hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) propellants. While significantly better than their predecessors, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) which were banned by the Montreal Protocol in 1987 due to effects on the ozone and subsequently phased as recently as 2008-HFC are potent greenhouse gases [[Citation 71](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. MDIs contribute to global warming, as HFCs have a high global warming potential (GWP), many folds worse compared to carbon dioxide [[Citation 72](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Dry powder inhalers (DPIs) and soft mist inhalers (SMIs) offer more environmentally friendly alternatives, as they do not use HFCs and have a lower carbon footprint [[Citation 73](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Additionally, the production, disposal, and recycling of inhaler devices also contribute to their environmental impact. Proper disposal and recycling programs can mitigate some of these effects, but widespread implementation remains a challenge [[Citation 74](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Efforts to develop and adopt inhalers with minimal environmental impact, such as those using alternative propellants or propellant-free technologies, are essential for reducing the ecological footprint of respiratory therapies.

### 2.6. Cost and (in)affordability

The high inhaler cost is a significant barrier to effective asthma and COPD management for many patients. Several factors contribute to this issue. A small number of large pharmaceutical companies dominate the market for inhalers with few generic options available. Patent protections on brand-name inhalers, which can get new patents with shuffling inhaler devices and drug type and dose, further restrict the availability of cheaper generic alternatives, further exacerbating the cost burden. The complexity of the inhaler mechanisms also adds to the production costs, which are passed on to consumers. Insurance coverage and pricing policies vary widely, leaving many patients with substantial out-of-pocket expenses. While there have been recent efforts in the US to address the at-times prohibitively expensive cost of inhaled medications, the cost disparity between the US and the United Kingdom for the same inhaler remains as high as 10-fold. [[Citation 75](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

## 3. Oral corticosteroids

Oral CSs are commonly used in the management of moderate (managed outpatient) and severe (requiring hospitalization) COPD exacerbations. While many clinicians offer intravenous or intramuscular administration, no benefit has been demonstrated compared to oral administration, as oral CS are rapidly absorbed, have high bioavailability, and rapid onset of peak serum levels within ~ 1 hour [[Citation 76](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 77](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Contrary to other indications for oral CS, dosing is not commonly weight-based. Instead, 40–60 mg prednisone for 5 days is commonly prescribed for COPD exacerbations based on data demonstrating decreased risk of intensive care unit and ventilatory support use, reduced rate of treatment failure, and improved FEV 1 and symptoms when compared to placebo (and no additional benefit but increased hyperglycemia when compared to 14 days of therapy) [[Citation 23](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 78](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. There is an increasing need identified for more personalized use of CS in COPD. The study of acute exacerbations and response (STARR2) study performed in the United Kingdom (UK) randomized standard therapy to doses targeted to blood eosinophils at the time of exacerbation. This non-inferiority trial showed no difference in the two arms but found lower cumulative oral CS dose in the blood eosinophil targeted group [[Citation 79](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

While there are clear benefits for systemic CS in COPD exacerbations, there is also risk with myriad adverse events that can occur acutely (hyperglycemia), sub acutely (pneumonia), or chronically (osteoporosis). Adverse events from oral CS include the risk of osteoporosis, fractures, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular/cerebrovascular disease, and all-cause mortality, are associated with increasing cumulative dose of oral CS [[Citation 80](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Even short-term bursts of oral CS are associated with an increased risk of pneumonia and mortality [[Citation 81](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Prescription of oral CS should be judiciously considered, balancing the severity of the exacerbation (and potential benefit) and patient-specific risks.

## 4. Phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitors in the treatment of COPD

Phosphodiesterase (PDE) enzymes metabolize cAMP and cGMP. There are 11 families of PDE, with PDE 3 and 4 of particular interest as pharmacologic targets for COPD due to their expression in airway smooth muscle and PDE4 presence in airway epithelial and inflammatory cells [[Citation 82](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Inhibition of these enzymes in the airways leads to bronchodilation, anti-inflammatory effects, improved airway clearance, and prevention of the bronchial wall remodeling that can occur in COPD. Furthermore, some of these effects are additive when PDE3/4 inhibitors are used in conjunction with other bronchodilators or glucocorticosteroids [[Citation 83](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. ### 4.1. Theophylline

The xanthine derivative theophylline is an oral, nonselective PDE inhibitor with a known narrow therapeutic window. It has been shown to have limited utility in the management of COPD. A randomized control trial investigating the addition of low-dose theophylline to inhaled corticosteroids in patients with COPD at high risk of exacerbation found it did not significantly reduce the rate of moderate-to-severe exacerbations over a 1-year period [[Citation 84](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. It did demonstrate a significant difference in the number of exacerbations treated in the hospital, most notably in a small subset of frequently hospitalized patients, but not in the number of non-COPD hospitalizations, nor episodes of pneumonia, lung function as measured by FEV 1, or measurements of quality of life or health status. Importantly, the use of theophylline as an adjunctive therapy was not associated with increased adverse reactions or events, or mortality [[Citation 84](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

A systematic review assessing the use of theophylline in stable COPD in 20 crossover, randomized controlled trials, found statistically significant improvement of lung function with an increase of 100 mL in FEV 1, ventilatory capacity, and arterial blood gas tensions [[Citation 85](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Additionally, patients preferred theophylline to placebo, despite a greater association with gastrointestinal side effects. There was no significant difference in distance walked, Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for breathlessness, symptoms of wheeze and dyspnea, or exacerbations. Notably, a majority of the included studies allowed concomitant use of other bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids, while some did not, and others did not specify [[Citation 85](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Theophylline was associated with significantly more nausea, while other side effects include headaches, insomnia, dyspepsia, and the potential for supraventricular arrhythmias [[Citation 85](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Theophylline is a challenging drug to use in practice due to many drug-interactions that influence its metabolism and require increased monitoring, notably including antibiotics such as erythromycin, clarithromycin, and quinolones, as well as disease states including heart failure, pneumonia, and viral infections [[Citation 86](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 4.2. Roflumilast

Roflumilast is an oral, selective PDE4 inhibitor that has been shown in large clinical trials to improve lung function and reduce rate of exacerbations in severe COPD, particularly in conjunction with long-acting bronchodilators, and in patients with a chronic bronchitis phenotype [[Citation 82](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

An early phase 3 trial and a large multiple-centered randomized controlled trial (RCT) (REACT) that evaluated oral roflumilast in combination LABA/ICS inhalers found moderately reduced COPD exacerbations and improvement in health-related quality of life measurements [[Citation 87](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 88](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A year-long, phase 4 trial (RE 2 SPOND) that randomized 2,354 COPD patients on LABA/ICS inhalers failed to show statistically significant reductions in moderate and/or severe COPD exacerbations [[Citation 89](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A small phase 2 RCT evaluated the effect of roflumilast added to standard COPD treatments [[Citation 90](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A small non-statistically significant greater increase in FEV 1 of 94 mL was seen at Day 28. The use of roflumilast compared to placebo significantly reduced the percentage of sputum neutrophils (−13.9%, 95% CI, −27.8% to −0.09%, _p_ = 0.018) [[Citation 90](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A systematic review of PDE4 inhibitors in the treatment of COPD included 34 separate RCTs evaluating roflumilast (20 trials with a total of 17,627 patients) and cilomilast (14 trials with a total of 6,457 patients) [[Citation 91](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The mean difference in FEV 1 over the trial period was 51.53 mL with the PDE4 inhibitors compared to placebo (95% CI, 43.17 to 59.90 mL), quality of life, and reduced COPD exacerbations (OR = 0.78, 95% CI, 0.73 to 0.83) [[Citation 91](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Like theophylline, roflumilast has a narrow therapeutic index, and is poorly tolerated due to gastrointestinal side effects [[Citation 92](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 4.3. Ensifentrine

More promising, is the advent of inhaled dual PDE3/4 inhibitors such as ensifentrine. Ensifentrine inhibits recombinant PDE3 approximately 3000-fold higher than it inhibits recombinant PDE 4 [[Citation 82](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Early studies with inhaled ensifentrine found that 3 mg twice-daily was able to improve peak FEV 1 in COPD patients [[Citation 93](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. It also improved symptoms [[Citation 94](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Improved FEV 1 was also seen when inhaled ensifentrine was added for patients on stable inhaled tiotropium [[Citation 95](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Preliminary phase 2 trials suggest improved symptoms, health-related quality of life, and sustained bronchodilation [[Citation 96](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

The ENHANCE trials are phase III randomized control trials that demonstrated the use of nebulized ensifentrine 3 mg twice-daily in patients with moderate-to-severe COPD led to significant improvement in lung function as measured by average FEV 1 area under the curve at 0–12 hours compared with placebo, along with improved symptoms and quality of life, reduced moderate-to-severe exacerbations, and increased time to first exacerbation. Importantly, these results were consistent regardless of the accompanying use of other COPD medications, and the medication was well tolerated without increased gastrointestinal adverse effects compared with the placebo [[Citation 97](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. It is delivered in a standard jet nebulizer with a mouthpiece twice-a-day by putting one 3 mg ampule in the nebulizer [[Citation 98](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. No significant drug interactions have been reported. Recent EMA and FDA approval of this new therapy has occurred and should be available soon. The most commonly reported side effects included hypertension, back pain, and urinary tract infections [[Citation 97](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

## 5. Antibiotics in the treatment of COPD

Given the role of respiratory infections in COPD exacerbations, the use of prophylactic antibiotics has been investigated and implemented for the reduction of exacerbations. In addition to their antibiosis, macrolides in particular demonstrate benefit via their anti-inflammatory properties, including reducing airway cytokine production [[Citation 99](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 100](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. They also interfere with biofilm formation, bacterial adherence of pathogens, and have a prokinetic activity on the GI tract that may reduce reflux and micro aspiration [[Citation 101](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Table 5 summarizes antibiotics commonly used prophylactically in COPD.

### 5.1. Erythromycin

A small, randomized control trial found that the use of erythromycin 125 mg three times daily for 6 months in patients with COPD resulted in a significant reduction of neutrophil count and activity in induced sputum, as well as in moderate-to-severe exacerbations and time to first exacerbation but did not show significant differences in health scores [[Citation 99](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The addition of erythromycin 250 mg twice daily for a year in patients with moderate-to-severe COPD has also demonstrated a significant reduction in exacerbation frequency, severity, and duration, without significant difference in FEV 1 decline, nor sputum inflammatory markers or bacteriology [[Citation 100](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. This study monitored for known potential adverse effects, excluding patients with QTc abnormalities on cardiogram, and found no changes in QTc interval or hepatic function tests with therapy, nor a significant difference in reported gastrointestinal side effects. Additionally, due to potential interaction with theophylline, patients taking this medication had serum levels monitored, without findings above therapeutic range [[Citation 100](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In addition to its interaction with theophylline, erythromycin is associated with a range of potential interactions, primarily related to CYP450, including, but not limited to, benzodiazepines, some immunosuppressants, statin therapy, methylprednisolone, and warfarin [[Citation 102](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 5.2. Azithromycin

Studies have shown azithromycin to be useful in reducing COPD exacerbations when added to standard therapy. A large, multicenter, randomized control trial found a hazard ratio of 0.73 (CI 0.63 to 0.84; _p_< 0.001) with the addition of azithromycin 250 mg daily for a year compared to placebo in patients with COPD at increased risk of exacerbation, as well as a prolonged time to first exacerbation (266 days in treatment group vs 174 days in placebo group, _p_< 0.001) [[Citation 103](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Similarly, the COLUMBUS trial found the addition of azithromycin 500 mg three times weekly for a year in patients with COPD with at least 3 or more exacerbations in the previous year by about 40% (unadjusted relative risk (RR) 0.6, CI 0.43–0.84; _p_ = 0.003). They also found treatment was associated with a significantly longer time to first exacerbation and about a 30% greater chance of remaining exacerbation-free at 6 months [[Citation 104](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In a small study investigating patients with severe COPD and tracheostomy, there were two exacerbations in a group of 11 patients treated with azithromycin 500 mg daily three times weekly at 3 months, versus 12 exacerbations in 10 patients on placebo [[Citation 105](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A systematic review performed by the European Respiratory Society (ERS) and American Thoracic Society (ATS) looked at four randomized control trials with varying macrolide regimens (erythromycin 200–400 mg daily, erythromycin 250 mg twice daily, azithromycin 250 mg daily, and azithromycin 500 mg 3 times weekly) for a year found a decreased rate of exacerbation (rate ratio 0.76) with a modest absolute decrease of 0.4 fewer exacerbations per patient per year, and overall recommended macrolide prophylaxis in patients with moderate-to-severe COPD and exacerbations despite optimal inhaled therapy [[Citation 61](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

A single-center retrospective observational study of COPD patients found that 126 patients prescribed azithromycin 250 mg at least three times weekly for 6 months had a significant decrease in the number of exacerbations (3.1 vs 2.3, _p_< 0.001) in the year after initiation, whereas 69 patients who were not prescribed antibiotic prophylaxis had significantly more exacerbations from 1 year to the next (1.7 vs 2.7, _p_< 0.001). Additionally, the treatment group continued to have significantly reduced exacerbations, Emergency Department (ED) visits, and hospital admissions beyond a year of follow-up. [[Citation 101](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Interestingly, a single-center retrospective study of the COLUMBUS cohort examining patients who continued azithromycin 500 mg three times weekly after a year for the study found no significant difference in exacerbation frequency compared to participants who discontinued azithromycin after the study, [[Citation 106](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. suggesting there may not be benefit of continued maintenance therapy past a year, but prospective trials are needed to further investigate. The BACE trial investigated the initiation of a loading dose of azithromycin 500 mg for 3 days in patients with COPD hospitalized for acute exacerbation in addition to standard antibiotic and steroid therapy, then maintained on azithromycin 250 mg every 2 days for 3 months and followed for another 6 months. In analyzing treatment failure, defined as the composite of treatment intensification with systemic corticosteroids and/or antibiotics, step-up in hospital care, or readmission for respiratory causes, they found an 18% reduction in treatment failure within 3 months, but it did not meet statistical significance as the study was underpowered due to small sample size [[Citation 107](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

A Cochrane systematic review of 14 studies with varying antibiotic regimens, including nine with daily macrolides, two with intermittent azithromycin (3 times weekly), one macrolide and one quinolone pulsed (5 days every 8 weeks), and one with arms comparing continuous doxycycline, intermittent azithromycin, and pulsed moxifloxacin with placebo, found a significant reduction in the number of patients with one or more exacerbations over the treatment period (OR 0.57, CI 0.42 to 0.78; 2716 participants across 10 studies). Notably, a subgroup analysis suggested continuous and intermittent regimens may be more effective than pulsed doses. Continuous and intermittent regimens also showed a significant reduction in the rate of exacerbations per patient per year [[Citation 108](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

In considering which patients may benefit most from azithromycin therapy, retrospective analyses have found it may be more effective in patients who are older and have milder GOLD stages, while it may have less utility in current smokers [[Citation 101](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 109](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Evidence also suggested treatment was better at preventing more severe exacerbations requiring intervention with both antibiotics and steroids [[Citation 109](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Despite the significant reduction in exacerbations, few studies have shown clinically significant improvement in quality of life. In Albert et. al, [[Citation 103](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. there was a significant decrease in the St. George Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), in which lower scores correspond to a higher quality of life, but it did not exceed the prespecified clinically significant difference of at least four. However, a higher proportion of patients (43%) in the treatment group did meet this difference compared with those in placebo (36%) [[Citation 103](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Severe COPD patients with tracheostomy did have a significant improvement in quality of life as measured by the Maugeri Respiratory Failure questionnaire (MRF26) when treated with azithromycin [[Citation 105](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The collaboration between ERS and ATS also demonstrated modest improvement in quality of life as measured by SGRQ with a mean difference less than four [[Citation 61](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In the case of the COLUMBUS trial, the improvement in SGRQ was not sustained at 12 months [[Citation 104](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Many studies with azithromycin excluded patients with hearing impairment, tachycardia, QTc prolongation, or risk of QTc prolongation at baseline. Some studies saw significant decrement in hearing in the treatment group, sometimes leading to premature discontinuation of therapy, although some patients had return to baseline hearing function with or without discontinuation of azithromycin [[Citation 61](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 103](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Gastrointestinal side effects, including diarrhea and stomachache, were commonly seen with the use of antibiotic therapy [[Citation 105](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 107](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. and in some cases led to discontinuation of therapy [[Citation 101](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In contrast to erythromycin, azithromycin does not appear to have many clinically significant drug interactions, probably because of its lack of complexation with CYP450 enzymes [[Citation 102](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

An important consideration with the use of chronic macrolide therapy is the concern for the development of antibiotic resistance. Albert et al. showed a decrease in colonization with selected respiratory pathogens, but in those who did become colonized, there was a significant increase in macrolide resistance [[Citation 103](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The ERS/ATS meta-analysis found inconclusive results regarding macrolide resistance, [[Citation 61](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. while the BACE trial saw no significant difference in newly acquired pathogens or macrolide-resistant bacteria in sputum cultures [[Citation 107](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Prophylactic macrolide therapy has shown to be effective in reducing exacerbations, leading to its use being recommended in the 2015 ACCP/CTS and 2017 ERS/ATS guidelines for patients with persistent exacerbations despite maintenance therapy [[Citation 61](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 110](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. However, both of these guidelines similarly suggest the use of roflumilast, although specifically in patients with COPD and a chronic bronchitis phenotype. No studies address the question of which medication clinicians should try first. A retrospective cohort analysis by Lam et al. used data from Veterans Health Administration (VHA) Corporate Data Warehouse (CDW) to compare outcomes in patients with COPD who were prescribed either roflumilast or azithromycin [[Citation 111](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. After adjusting for baseline differences, they found azithromycin was associated with slightly improved survival outcomes, while roflumilast had a higher risk of COPD-related (HR 1.21) and all-cause hospitalization (HR 1.23) [[Citation 111](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The ongoing RELIANCE randomized control trial is aiming to further elucidate the comparison between these therapeutic options [[Citation 110](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 5.3. Moxifloxacin

The PULSE Study group performed a randomized control trial with findings that the addition of moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 5 days every 8 weeks for 6 courses compared with placebo in stable patients with COPD reduced the odds of exacerbation by 20% in the intention to treat population (_p_ = 0.059), 25% among the per protocol population (_p_ = 0.046), and 45% in per protocol patients with purulent or mucopurulent sputum at baseline (_p_ = 0.006). There was no significant difference in hospitalization rates, mortality, lung function, changes in SGRQ total scores, and no evidence of the development of moxifloxacin resistance. However, for patients colonized with _P. aeruginosa_ at baseline, there was an increase in the median MIC for moxifloxacin, suggesting against the use of moxifloxacin in this population. There were significantly more adverse effects in the treatment group, including discontinuation of moxifloxacin due to gastrointestinal effects [[Citation 112](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In addition to GI side effects, moxifloxacin, like other fluoroquinolones, comes with a risk for arrhythmia, and dysglycemia [[Citation 113](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 5.4. Doxycycline

A randomized, placebo-controlled trial investigating the use of doxycycline 100 mg daily for a year did not show a significant reduction in the rate of exacerbation (RR, 0.86; CI 0.67–1.10; _p_ = 0.23), but a subgroup analysis did show significant reduction in patients with severe COPD (RR 0.36; CI 0.15–0.85; _p_ = 0.019) and serum eosinophils less than 300 cells/µl (RR 0.50; CI 0.29–0.84; _p_ = 0.01). There was no significant difference in the rate of treated exacerbations, number of hospitalizations, time to first exacerbation, FEV 1, or adverse events. However, health status as measured by SGRQ was significantly worse in the treatment group, and there were more gastrointestinal disorders seen with doxycycline, although this was not statistically significant [[Citation 114](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Other considerations of doxycycline use include adverse effects including esophageal injury, bone growth inhibition, and photosensitivity, along with drug interactions with divalent cations, iron, anticonvulsants, rifampin, and warfarin [[Citation 115](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

## 6. Biologicals/monoclonal antibodies (MAB) in the treatment of COPD

The asthma-COPD overlap syndrome (ACOS or ACO) has been recognized for more than a decade now [[Citation 116–119](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Type 2 (Th2) lymphocyte inflammatory-mediated airway constriction is thought to be important in asthma and in ACOS [[Citation 116](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. When Th2 lymphocytes are activated, dendritic cells, basophils, macrophages, mast cells and eosinophils contribute to the amplification of the pathological inflammatory pathways that include interleukins (IL) such as IL-5, IL-4 and IL-14. Monoclonal antibodies directed to components of this inflammatory cascade have been developed and approved for asthma with some tested in COPD patients (Tables 6 and 7). Most of these studies have focused on ACOS patients with evidence of Th2-mediated inflammation, such as elevated blood eosinophil counts or IgE levels. Newer agents are looking at non-Th2 traditional mechanisms of mediated inflammation in asthma and COPD.
