The treatment of cystic fibrosis has been revolutionized by drugs that work on the cystic fibrosis conductance regulator (CFTR). The CFTR is potentially damaged by cigarette smoking [[Citation 135](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The acquired dysfunction of CFTR is thought to lead to airway obstruction, chronic airway inflammation and bacterial colonization by reducing airway surface liquid and decreased mucociliary transport [[Citation 135](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 136](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Drugs that effect and improve the CFTR dysfunction associated with smoking are being evaluated in COPD patients.

### 6.1. Omalizumab

Omalizumab is approved for refractory asthma (Table 6). It is a humanized murine IgG MAB with binding to the CH3 domain of IgE [[Citation 134](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The binding by omalizumab to IgE prevents IgE binding to mast cells, basophils, dendritic cells and monocytes reducing Th2-mediated inflammation. A large prospective, real-world study evaluating omalizumab in asthmatics called the PROSERO trial included 106 patients who met various definitions of ACOS [[Citation 120](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 137](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. They showed that omalizumab treatment in these ACOS patients decreased the rate of exacerbations and improved Asthma Control Test (ACT) scores over the 48-week trial [[Citation 120](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In another study, 10 ACOS patients treated with omalizumab had a significant reduction in eosinophils and serum IL-4 levels compared to baseline levels along with improved FEV 1 and ACT scores [[Citation 138](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A small study of 3 ACOS patients treated with omalizumab had improved ACT scores, reduced exacerbations, and reduced hospitalizations after 1 year compared to their baseline [[Citation 139](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Maltby and colleagues [[Citation 121](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. reviewed the Australian Xolair Registry and identified 17 ACOS patients that had been treated with omalizumab for at least 6 months [[Citation 121](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Compared to baseline, their spirometry did not improve but ACT and asthma quality of life scores improved. These relative low-quality studies without an RCT suggests that ACOS patients with elevated serum eosinophil counts may see a modest improvement with omalizumab. Further phase 3 RCTs with very defined phenotypes are needed to establish the role of omalizumab is in eosinophilic associated COPD.

### 6.2. Anti-IL-5/IL-5 R

As many as 20–40% of patients with COPD have ACOS manifesting as a type of eosinophilic COPD [[Citation 140](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Because of their efficacy as an add-on medication in Th2-mediated asthma, anti-IL-5 and IL-5 MAB receptor antagonists have been explored in eosinophilic COPD. Two phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group trials evaluated mepolizumab in eosinophilic COPD patients. These trials were called METREX (100 mg subcutaneous (sc) mepolizumab every 4 weeks for 52 weeks) and METEREO (100 mg or 300 mg sc every 4 weeks for 52 weeks) [[Citation 122](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. All patients had to have at least 150 blood eosinophil cells/μL at screening or at least 300 blood eosinophil cells/μL during the previous year. The 100 mg dose of mepolizumab was found to lower the rate of COPD exacerbations compared to placebo [[Citation 122](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. These findings were confirmed when a meta-analysis of 1136 individual patient data from the 52-week METREX and METRED studies were combined [[Citation 55](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A single-centered, retrospective, observational study of 20 elderly (age >65 years old) with COPD and at least 150 eosinophils cells per milliliter at baseline or >300 eosinophils cells/μL during the last year were treated with mepolizumab. The number of exacerbations in the previous 6 months were annualized and compared to the exacerbations 24 weeks also annualized after the mepolizumab was started. Clinically significant reductions in the COPD exacerbation rate and blood eosinophils were reported [[Citation 123](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. These studies suggest that patients with eosinophilic COPD or ACOS are likely to respond to the MAB mepolizumab which binds IL-5 and prevents its binding to the receptor and improves these patients [[Citation 141](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Another MAB, benralizumab blocks the IL-5 receptor and has been tested in a phase 2a study of COPD patients with eosinophilia [[Citation 124](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In this study, 100 mg benralizumab or placebo were randomized and given to 101 COPD patients with eosinophilia for at least 48 weeks. There was no reduction in COPD exacerbation noted in this study. Two phase 3 trials with benralizumab called GALATHEA and TERRANOVA in 2665 COPD patients with eosinophils at three different levels (>300, 220–299, and <220 cells/μL) were treated with placebo or 10, 30, or 100 mg benralizumab sc every 8 weeks were reported [[Citation 125](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The primary endpoint was annualized exacerbation rates determined at week 56 in patients with eosinophil counts >220 cells/μL. The use of benralizumab was not associated with reduced exacerbation in the group with eosinophils >220 cells/μL. Two retrospective analyses have been done on the GALATHEA and TERANOVA data. When the 100 mg sc benralizumab every 8 weeks group with blood eosinophils greater than or equal to 220 cells/μL at baseline or a history of more than 3 exacerbations in the year prior were analyzed, there was a reduction in exacerbations and improved spirometry [[Citation 142](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Another post-hoc analysis of these two large studies evaluated COPD patients with blood eosinophil >300 cells/μL and who had at least one exacerbation after randomization [[Citation 143](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Those treated with 100 mg sc benralizumab (_N_ = 73) and placebo (_N_ = 72) met the above definitions and after their first exacerbation, benralizumab treatment significantly reduced further exacerbations at both 30 days and 90 days compared to placebo. Several meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and real-world retrospective studies have also suggested IL-5 MAB-directed therapy has efficacy in eosinophilic COPD phenotype [[Citation 140](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 144](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 145](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Further studies such as the phase 3 RESOLUTE or ABRA trial [[Citation 143](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. are being done to explore if this or other COPD phenotypes will be responsive to benralizumab.

### 6.3. Anti-IL-4/IL-13 antagonist MABs

The fully human MAB dupilumab blocks the IL-4 and IL-13 pathways and has been approved for asthma (Table 6). Two large phase 3 trials have evaluated dupilumab in COPD patients with increased blood eosinophilia. The first trial (BOREAS) had 939 COPD patients with blood eosinophil of >300 per milliliter at screening and counts >230 cells/μL at randomization. They were treated with placebo or dupilumab 300 mg sc as an add-on therapy every 2 weeks for 52 weeks [[Citation 50](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Significant reduction in exacerbations and improved quality of life were found with those treated with dupilumab. A recent pre-publication of the NOTUS Trial has been released [[Citation 50](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In this trial, 935 COPD patients with screening blood eosinophil count >300 cells/μL were randomized to placebo or dupilumab 300 mg sc every 2 weeks for 52 weeks. The rate of annualized moderate-to-severe exacerbations was significantly reduced with dupilumab (RR = 0.66 (95% CI, 0.54–0.82, _p_ = 0.001)). A significant increase in FEV 1 was noted in the dupilumab group at weeks 12 and 52 [[Citation 127](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In this COPD phenotype, dupilumab appears to be efficacious with no major adverse events.

### 6.4. TSLP blocker

Tezepelumab is a IgG21 and a MAB that blocks the activity of the epithelial cytokine thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP). It is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in the treatment of asthma [[Citation 146](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A recent phase 2a trial in 333 patients with moderate to very severe COPD treated with placebo or 420 mg Tezepelumab subcutaneously every 4 weeks for up to 52 weeks [[Citation 130](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Those patients with COPD and baseline blood eosinophils >150 cells/μL given tezepelumab had a significant 37% reduction in exacerbations compared to placebo. Further phase 3 trials to better understand the potential efficacy of tezepelumab in eosinophilia associated COPD are needed.

### 6.5. Anti – IL − 33

In addition to mitigating IL-5, IL-4, IL-13 and TSLP, MABs that block IL-33 have been proposed to treat Th2-mediated COPD in a step toward precision medicine [[Citation 147](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Tozorakimab (MED13506) is a potent human MAB that inhibits both reduced and oxidized IL-33 through action on serum-stimulated 2 (ST2) and the receptor for advanced glycation end products/epidermal growth factor receptor (RAGE/E6FR complex) signaling pathways [[Citation 148](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A phase 1, first-in-human, randomized, double-blind study evaluated safety, tolerability, immunogenicity, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of sc and intravenous doses in 56 healthy participants with a history of mild atopy getting a single escalating dose of tozorakimab [[Citation 128](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A second part of the study included 24 patients with mild COPD who received multiple ascending doses of subcutaneous tozorakimab or placebo. Tozorakimab was well tolerated and demonstrated engagement with serum and nasal endogenous IL-33. The mean serum half-life was 11.7–17.3 days. It significantly reduced IL-5 and IL-13 serum levels in patients with COPD compared to placebo and was well tolerated [[Citation 128](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Itepekimab is another human IgG4 MAB that is an anti-IL-33 agent. A phase 2a trial evaluated Itepekimab 300 mg given as two sc injections every 2 weeks for 24–52 weeks compared to placebo in 343 current or former smokers diagnosed with COPD in the last year [[Citation 129](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A numerical but not statistically significant reduction in the annualized rates of exacerbation was seen with itepekimab (RR = 0.81 (95% CI 0.61–1.07, _p_ = 0.13)). In a subgroup analysis of former smokers with COPD, the reduction in COPD exacerbations reached statistical significance (RR = 0.58 (CI 95%, 0.39–0,85, _p_ = 0.0061)). No changes in FEV 1 or adverse events was noted. Two phase 3 randomized controlled trials in former smokers with moderate-to-severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and >1 moderate-to-severe exacerbations in the last year (AERIFY-1/2) comparing itepekimab 300 mg sc every 2 weeks to placebo are ongoing with completion dates estimated to be around October 2025 [[Citation 149](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Although promising, the role of IL-33 MAB therapy in COPD remains to be defined but the ongoing phase 3 itepekimab trials may help answer the question.

### 6.6. Active monoclonal antibodies and current COPD trials

A search of clinical trials.gov for monoclonal antibody treatments and COPD found registered trials for benralizumab and mepolizumab. The monoclonal antibody CM310, a humanized anti-IL-4 and IL-13 antibody is also being studied in COPD patients. A small safety and pharmacokinetic study of andecaliximab has finished in COPD subjects. Andecaliximab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits metalloproteinase 9 that in turn, inhibits remodeling and tumor growth. A large study of 343 COPD subjects received SAR440340 (REGN3500) or placebo. SAR440340 is an IL-33 directed antibody that is also being evaluated for asthma. Subjects with bronchitis and COPD have had the safety and efficacy tested using the fully human anti-IL-8 monoclonal antibody. It is likely that many new monoclonal antibodies focused toward inflammation will be tested.

### 6.7. Cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator potentiators

An acquired dysfunction in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) induced from smoking, inflammation, and infection in some COPD patients has been reported [[Citation 136](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The dysfunction of the CFTR is about 50% in COPD and chronic bronchitis patients compared to that found in cystic fibrosis patients [[Citation 136](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. As a result of this CFTR dysfunction, CFTR potentiators used in the treatment of cystic fibrosis have been suggested as a treatment for COPD patients, particularly those with chronic bronchitis. A phase 2, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in moderate-to-severe COPD patients evaluated the CFTR potentiator icenticaftor as a proof-of-concept trial [[Citation 135](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A total of 92 COPD patients were randomized (2:1) to icenticaftor 300 mg or placebo twice-a-day for 29 days with additional 4 weeks in which all subjects received placebo twice-a-day [[Citation 135](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. No change in lung clearance index was found with the CFTR potentiator but a mean increase of 50 mL in pre-bronchodilator FEV 1 and a mean increase of 63 mL after bronchodilator was seen when icenticaftor was used compared to placebo. Large phase 3 trials with increased phenotypical specificity are needed to define the potential role of CFTR potentiators in the treatment of COPD.

## 7. Mucolytics

A number of mucolytics have been used in the treatment of COPD and its phenotypes. Excess sputum production and chronic bronchitis are common in COPD and during COPD exacerbations. A recent study of 4,363 COPD subjects followed for a median of 9.5 years found that mortality was increased as a function of lung segments with mucous plugs on chest CT scan [[Citation 150](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. N-acetylcysteine (NAC), ambroxol, erdosteine, bromhexine, high molecular weight hyaluronan, and hypertonic saline have been used in treating COPD patients [[Citation 151](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Routes of dosing have included intravenous (IV), oral or nebulized depending on the agent and the study. A Cochrane systematic review found with moderate confidence, that NAC, carbocysteine, and erdosteine were associated with reduction in disability days [[Citation 152](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In addition, the meta-analysis of 28 studies including 6,723 patients found that treatment with mucolytics may be more likely to be exacerbation-free (OR = 1.73, 95% CI 1.56–1.91) but with only moderate-certainty. [[Citation 152](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

A pairwise network meta-analyses of 2,753 COPD patients in 7 RTCs that included oral dosing of erdosteine (600 mg/day), carbocysteine (1500 mg/day), and NAC (1200 mg/day) found that these mucolytics with antioxidant properties reduced the risk of acute exacerbations of COPD (AECOPD) (RR = 0.74, 95% CI 0.68–0.80) [[Citation 153](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In this study, erdosteine was most effective, followed by carbocysteine, and then NAC. The study further noted that only erdosteine significantly reduced the risk of experiencing at least one AECOPD (_p_< 0.01) and the chance of AECOP hospitalization (_p_< 0.05). A meta-analysis of 24 RCTs with 2,192 COPD patients that included studies with NAC, ambroxol, erdosteine, bromhexine, hypertonic saline and high molecular weight hyaluronan was performed [[Citation 151](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Increased treatment success (RR = 1.37, 95% CI 1.08–1.73), symptom improvement (standardized mean difference (SMD) = 0.86, 95% CI 0.63–1.09), and reduced cough at follow-up (RR = 1.93, 95% CI 1.15–3.23) was seen.

### 7.1. Erdosteine

Erdosteine, (_N_-(carboxymethylthioacetyl)-homocysteine thiolactone) is approved by the EMA but not the FDA originally as a mucolytic and more recently, for the treatment of mercury toxicities [[Citation 154](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The thiol groups are thought to be the active sites after metabolism. It is thought, in addition to being mucolytic, to have antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-bacterial effects [[Citation 154](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

The RESTORE trial evaluated erdosteine 300 mg orally, twice-a-day in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 467 COPD patients over 12 months with AECOPD as the primary endpoint [[Citation 155](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A reduction in AECOPD events of 19.4% was seen going from 1.13 AEOPD per year to 0.91 AECOPD event per year (_p_ = 0.01). The effect was primarily because of the drug’s effect on mild rather than moderate-to-severe AECOPD. The duration of AECOPD events was significantly reduced with erdosteine treatment by 24.6% across the spectrum of mild-to-severe exacerbations (9.55 versus 12.63 days, _p_ = 0.023) [[Citation 155](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Two RCT’s have demonstrated erdosteine’ s ability to reduce oxidative stress in COPD patients including during exercise [[Citation 156](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 157](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Post hoc analyses of the RESTORE trial confirmed that adding erdosteine to usual COPD maintenance treatment also reduces the number of mild AECOPD, their duration, and the number of episodes requiring antibiotics [[Citation 158](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 159](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

### 7.2. N-acetylcysteine (NAC)

NAC is a glutathione replacement used IV and orally in the treatment of acetaminophen overdoses to protect the liver and other organs. It can also be nebulized to thin mucous or used with direct infusion by bronchoscope to break up mucous plugs. In addition to this mucolytic effect, NAC is an antioxidant drug. It is a ‘direct’ scavenger of reactive oxygen species and an indirect antioxidant by providing cysteine which is a critical precursor in the synthesis of intracellular glutathione [[Citation 160](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

The Chinese trial PANTHEON included 1,006 COPD patients that were randomized to NAC 600 mg orally twice-a-day or placebo. PANTHEON was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study [[Citation 160](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The year-long trial reported that the AECOPD rate was 1.16 AECOPD per patients-year in the NAC treated group and 1.49 AECOPD per patients-year in the placebo group (RR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.67–0.90, _p_ = 0.011). NAC was also found to be well tolerated [[Citation 160](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

A single-center, retrospective cohort study in 453 COPD patients who had an AECOPD requiring hospitalization were assigned to an inhaled NAC group or a non-NAC group. A total of 192 of these patients were propensity matched. A composite endpoint of in-hospital mortality, need for mechanical ventilation, and readmission for COPD within 30 days was used. The primary combined endpoint was found to be 5.2% for the NAC treated group compared to 16.7% for the propensity matched control (_p_ = 0.011) [[Citation 161](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Another small single center, randomized, double-blind prospective trial in 120 COPD patients compared treatment for 6 months with NAC 600 mg orally-a-day with propolis (shown to increase tissue regeneration, anti-inflammation, antioxidant, and having some antimicrobial effects), 600 mg NAC twice-a-day with propolis, or placebo [[Citation 162](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. The NAC 600 mg/day with propolis treated groups showed variable improvement in symptoms and the NAC 1200 mg/day with propolis showed significantly less exacerbations compared to placebo. Another study evaluated NAC 600 mg/day plus 80 mg propolis, NAC 1200 mg/day plus 160 mg propolis or placebo in COPD patients with frequent exacerbations. This small study of 46 patients for 12 months found that the AECOPD incidence rate was 52.6% in those treated with placebo, 15.4% in those patients treated with NAC 600 mg/day plus 80 mg propolis/day, and 7.1% in the highest dosed group (1200 mg NAC/160 mg propolis/day, (_p_ = 0.013) [[Citation 163](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

The BRONCUS trial randomized 523 COPD patients to 600 mg NAC orally daily or placebo. The patients were followed for 3 years. The primary outcomes were change in FEV 1 and rates of COPD exacerbations [[Citation 164](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. This study reported no difference in the FEV 1, decline or in the number of COPD exacerbations per year between the NAC treated and placebo treated groups. A subgroup analysis of COPD patients not taking inhaled corticosteroids suggested that those taking NAC had fewer COPD exacerbations (0.96 per year versus 1.29 per year, Hazard Ratio (HR) = 0.79, 95% CI 0.631–0.989, _p_ = 0.04) [[Citation 164](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

Several meta-analyses and systematic reviews have focused on NAC therapy in COPD patients. A report using 12 trials, and 2,691 COPD patients found that both high-dose and low-dose NAC reduced exacerbations when given >6 months but not when given short-term NAC [[Citation 165](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. No effect on FEV 1, FVC, or inspiratory capacity was seen with NAC. Another systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies published in English found improvement in FEV 1 and FEV 1 /FVC with NAC treatment [[Citation 166](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. In addition to the spirometry improvement, COPD-related symptoms improved. An additional meta-analysis in nine RCTs with 1,076 COPD patients was used in this study. No significant change or difference in symptoms, pulmonary function decay, number or rate of exacerbations was seen [[Citation 167](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. A recent meta-analysis of trials using NAC treatment in COPD and chronic bronchitis patients used 20 studies. The incidence of exacerbations as compared to placebo decreased (incidence rate ratio (IRR) = 0.76, 05% CI 0.59–0.99). NAC treatments greater than 5 months confirmed these results [[Citation 168](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)]. Variable results in meta-analyses suggest significant study design and patient phenotype differences. A reduction in COPD exacerbations seems to be consistently reported with oral NAC when used longer than 5–6 months but reductions in spirometry declines are not as consistently found with oral NAC treatment in COPD patients.

## 8. Expert opinion

The understanding of the complex syndrome of COPD and its various endotypes and phenotypes continues to expand. With this expansion, new pharmacological therapeutic options emerge, and old options become more precisely applied. Routine inhalers both short- and long-acting anti-muscarinics and beta2-agonists delivered by dry powder, metered doses, spring driven mist inhalers to nebulizer-based medications are key treatments. Single-device combination inhaler therapies, including SABA/SAMA, LAMA/LABA, LABA/ICS, and LAMA/LABA/ICS, are available and have reduced the burden of dosing frequency and difficulty for patients leading to improved compliance. The use of MAB therapy, particularly dupilumab, is an exciting option to curb exacerbation frequency and slow lung decline in patients Th2 inflammation. Improved agents targeting known pathway such as the recently FDA-approved inhaled PDE 3/4 inhibitor ensifentrine have arisen demonstrating benefit with fewer off-target effects.

Despite the hope gained by the new medications available, there is considerable work to be done to improve how care is delivered to patients with COPD. Barriers include immediacy bias (treating exacerbations without an eye on future suppression), high cost (unaffordable inhaled medications), access to care, and perhaps most difficult to address, a history of nihilism that has shrouded COPD care and patients. The use of azithromycin stands testament to the lack of medications not being the entire problem. For over a decade, there has been considerable evidence from multiple randomized clinical trials demonstrating benefit from azithromycin in suppressing COPD exacerbation frequency by 20–30%, yet very few patients who meet criteria actually get prescribed this affordable and well-tolerated drug [[Citation 101](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#),[Citation 103–109](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2024.2409322#)].

With more to offer select groups patients with COPD, clinicians and health systems need to change their approach. With more nuances of care and specialty needs (e.g. respiratory therapist assessment of adequate drug delivery and technique, MAB education and administration), it is likely there will be a rise in COPD-focused clinics. For all clinicians, there will need to adapt to this rapidly changing field by educating themselves on identifying the treatable phenotypes and endotypes of disease. Clinics and clinicians are only a piece: institutions will need to develop approaches to manage COPD patients at every touch point in the system (clinic, hospital, emergency department, lab, etc.) and support the infrastructure needed for the aforementioned targeted care.

The pharmacotherapeutics for the COPD patient have evolved dramatically in the last 20 years. We anticipate even more new therapeutic potions to come in the next 20 years, hopefully with the necessary clinical reorientation on how COPD is managed. As enthusiasm for more effective medicines spur the field toward personalized medicine, our hope is that equal effort is paid to screening, prevention (smoking cessation), social determinants of health, and access to care so this benefit both equitably and cost-effectively improves the care of COPD patients.

## Article highlights

*   Treatment options for the COPD patient continue to evolve and become more complicated.

*   In addition to inhaled short- and long-acting anti-muscarinics and beta2-agonists, inhaled corticosteroids appear to provide excellent treatment to the COPD patient with elevated eosinophils.

*   Phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitors have a long history of use in COPD treatment but an inhaled PDE 3/4 inhibitor ensifentrine has recently been approved by both EMA and FDA and adds an additional therapeutic option.

*   The asthma-COPD overlap syndrome or phenotype is frequently a type 2 lymphocyte inflammatory-mediated airway constriction process and monoclonal antibody (MAB) therapies improve outcomes in some patients. The anti-IL-4/IL-13 antagonist MAB dupilumab is thought to be effective in COPD patients with elevated eosinophilia.
